widgets_values:
Fourier playground: filtering in the frequency domain

cv2.dft (flags = DFT_COMPLEX_OUTPUT) turns the float grayscale into a 2-channel (re, im) spectrum. The 'Spectrum view' subgraph renders the standard figure: magnitude -> log(1 + m) -> 'CV Roll (FFT Shift)' so the zero frequency sits in the CENTER (cv2 puts it in the top-left corner). Frequency masks are drawn in that centered layout with plain drawing nodes; the 'Frequency mask filter' subgraph then fftshifts the spectrum to match, zeroes everything outside the mask (cv2.copyTo), shifts back and inverse-transforms (idft, DFT_SCALE | DFT_REAL_OUTPUT).

LOW-PASS: keep a centered disc -> only slow intensity changes survive (blur). HIGH-PASS: the inverted disc -> only edges/texture survive (the mean goes too, so the preview is normalized).

NOTCH FILTER: the bottom rows synthesize PERIODIC noise - a vertical sine pattern built from the remap Identity Map's x-coordinate ramp (cv2.polarToCart turns magnitude-1 + angle into cos/sin) - and add it onto the photo. In the spectrum the stripes are just TWO bright spikes, mirrored about the center on the horizontal axis (at u = width/period, here width/16). Punching two small black discs exactly there (the notch mask) erases the stripes almost perfectly while the photo itself keeps all its other frequencies - compare the two PSNR readouts.

widgets_values:
Periodic noise removal - OpenCV tutorial 'Periodic Noise Removing Filter'
https://docs.opencv.org/5.0/tutorials/imgproc/periodic_noise_removing_filter/periodic_noise_removing_filter.html

period_input.jpg is a halftone-screened newspaper photo: the printing
screen is a PERIODIC pattern, so in the Fourier domain it is a handful of
bright spikes rather than something spread out. Punch a disk of zeros out
of the spectrum at each spike (a NOTCH REJECT filter) and the screen goes
away while the picture stays.

TWO DETECTORS RUN SIDE BY SIDE, and neither types a coordinate.
'Detect Spectral Peaks' is the tuned one: a noise spike is a statistical
OUTLIER, so the cut is mean + sigmas * std of the log spectrum, and
regions under min_area are dropped. 'Detect Spectral Peaks (K-Means)'
has neither knob: the cut is the maximum the noise floor could reach
across N pixels (the floor of a power spectrum is exponential, which
fixes both constants), and what survives it is split by k-means with
K=2 over (peak prominence, area). 8 notches against 10, and 0.9710
against 0.9701 on the tutorial's published output.

NOTHING HERE TYPES A COORDINATE. The tutorial hard-codes three notch
centres; 'CV Detect Spectral Peaks' reads them off the log PSD instead -
a noise spike is a statistical OUTLIER in the log spectrum, so the cut is
mean + 3.5 standard deviations of the spectrum itself. It finds the
same three families the hand-measured list had, and the result matches
the tutorial's published output (period_result.jpg) at 0.971 either way,
against 0.737 for the input.

That the coordinates have to be FOUND rather than copied is the point:
the tutorial's own (705, 458), (850, 391) and (993, 325) are all past the
right edge of the 640x471 image it ships them with. A spectral coordinate
is a position in a spectrum of a given size and does not survive a
rescale - the same trap as the R=53 disk radius in the out-of-focus
deblur tutorial.

TO OVERRIDE: 'notches' is just an Nx3 (x, y, radius) array. Drop a
'CV Points' node in front of the filter with rows like [403, 174, 21] to
place them by hand, or 'CV Concat Arrays' to add one to what was found.

widgets_values:
Wiener Filter (deblur) - OpenCV tutorial 'Out-of-focus Deblur Filter'
https://docs.opencv.org/5.0/tutorials/imgproc/out_of_focus_deblur_filter/out_of_focus_deblur_filter.html

Formula: Hw = Re(H) / (Re(H)^2 + 1/SNR), H = DFT of a normalised disk PSF.
R = PSF radius in PIXELS, SNR = signal-to-noise ratio.

The input is SYNTHETIC (generated for this pack): a 634x716 crop
of text_page_shadow.jpg convolved with a disk of radius 6 plus a little
sensor noise, so the number to type into R is known exactly instead of
guessed - and text_page_sharp.jpg is the same crop unblurred, the ground
truth to compare the result against.

R IS A LENGTH, SO IT ONLY MEANS ANYTHING AT ONE RESOLUTION.
The tutorial quotes R=53 / SNR=5200 for its own original.jpg. Those numbers
do NOT transfer: the file it ships is a ~9x downscaled 640x480 copy of the
photo they were measured on, whose real disk radius is 6 px (re-blurring the
tutorial's own recovered.jpg with a disk of radius 6 reproduces its blurred
input at unit gain, RMSE 3.4/255; R=53 gives 19.0). Feeding R=53 to a
640x480 image amplifies ~9x too much and clips to black and white. Always
measure R at the resolution you are actually filtering.

SNR is dimensionless and does transfer. Raise it for sharpness, lower it
(500..1000) for less ringing.

GREYSCALE vs COLOUR: cv2.dft is single-channel, so the colour variant runs
one Wiener per channel and merges the three RAW float fields before a SINGLE
min-max stretch - stretching each channel on its own would map three
different ranges onto 0..255 and shift the colour balance.

Both branches saturate to 0..255 before that stretch, the same
convertTo(CV_8U) + normalize(NORM_MINMAX) pair the tutorial ends with, so
feed them 0..255 data ('uint8 (0-255)' on 'CV Image -> Array').

The wrap-around ringing along the borders is inherent to filtering in the
frequency domain; the tutorial notes it too and points at edge tapering as
the fix, which this graph does not do.

nodes.title: B: recolour the luma from the blurred source

widgets_values:
TWO WAYS TO GET COLOUR BACK (lanes 2 and 3 below)

A. Deconvolve all three channels. cv2.dft is single-channel, so the
   colour subgraph runs the mono one per channel and stretches the three
   'raw' float fields TOGETHER (three separate stretches = a colour
   cast). Three DFT pairs instead of one.

B. Deconvolve the LUMA only, then re-colour that grayscale result with
   'Colorize Superpixels (FLANN)', using the BLURRED colour source as
   the reference: chroma survives a smear far better than luma detail,
   so the blurred original is a perfectly good palette.

nodes.title: A: deblurred per channel (3 DFT pairs)

widgets_values:
Wiener Filter (motion deblur) - OpenCV tutorial 'Motion Deblur Filter'
https://docs.opencv.org/5.0/tutorials/imgproc/motion_deblur_filter/motion_deblur_filter.html

Same Wiener kernel as the out-of-focus filter (wiener_filter_test.json),
Hw = Re(H) / (Re(H)^2 + 1/SNR); only the PSF differs - a LINE of LEN
pixels at THETA degrees instead of a disk, drawn as an ellipse with a
zero-width axis. The image is edge-tapered first, or the DFT's circular
wrap rings the left and right borders into stripes.

LEN is a LENGTH and only means anything at ONE resolution: the tutorial
quotes LEN=125 / LEN=78 for licence-plate photos it does not ship. Here
the smear was applied by us, so
LEN=21 / THETA=15 are exact by construction and SNR=50 is the
value that agrees best with text_page_sharp.jpg, the same crop unblurred.
